dropped_turns.speaker: PRO
dropped_turns.text: Consider an official supplier whose easy contracts disappear when outside partners withdraw. He must either support harmful policy without those rewards or press for a different course. That proves isolation reaches the incentives behind aggression.

dropped_turns.speaker: CON
dropped_turns.text: If you admit humanitarian safeguards are needed, who decides which families qualify before trade, travel, and contact are cut? Why trust a broad isolation policy to avoid the very harm you describe?

dropped_turns.speaker: PRO
dropped_turns.text: Humanitarian channels can be defined around essential goods and family needs, so the premise that every connection is cut is false. The broader point remains: leaders should lose normal access until harmful conduct ends.

turns.speaker: MOD

They should address each other directly, and I may keep the discussion on the question.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Isolation is not hatred of ordinary people; it is a refusal to make normal business excuse aggression. When access remains easy, pressure fades and leaders learn that disruption carries no real cost for their choices. We should isolate Russia to set a clear boundary. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Let Wendy respond to it.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Isolation sounds firm, but it can trap ordinary families while leaving powerful decision makers insulated. Keeping limited contact protects routes for aid, dialogue, and future change. turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Round two is where the debaters address one another in turn. This round runs two and a half minutes from the moment I finish. I will call ten seconds before the end.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Imagine a parent needing medicine that arrives through ordinary trade. A blanket isolation blocks that route before it changes any leader's conduct. That proves isolation punishes civilians more reliably than power.

turns.speaker: PRO

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: When isolation would block food, medicine, or family contact, it is wrong because the burden falls first on people without control. In that condition, limited targeted pressure is better.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Limited contact can help a family in a hard case, and I would protect humanitarian channels. But broad economic and political distance removes the normal rewards leaders use; that pressure supports isolation.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your humanitarian exception raises another problem: students in joint art programs may lose mentors, travel plans, and shared performances. Those personal exchanges need careful permits, because young creators should not carry adults' disputes.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: But we're getting a little bit off the isolation of Russia from the wider world.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The question is whether Russia should be isolated, and I say no because broad separation harms people who cannot alter policy. Keep pressure focused on responsible decision makers, not entire communities.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: When banks, firms, and official channels withdraw, leaders lose easy ways to fund and normalize harmful actions. That loss forces a choice between continued aggression and renewed cooperation. It proves isolation creates leverage.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Cultural ties also matter: families speak across borders, and small exchanges preserve trust for later repair. But the motion asks about isolation; how does cutting normal ties hurt leaders before ordinary people?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: It hurts leaders by denying them revenue, access, and prestige; humanitarian safeguards can shield ordinary people. Your claim treats normal ties as harmless, yet those ties can finance the very pressure you-

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Countries need working connections with the outside world, because isolation rarely produces wiser choices from those in power. The people who face its daily costs are usually the least able to change policy.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Your claim that isolation rarely changes leaders is the weakest point, because leaders depend on money, access, and recognition. Removing those supports does not guarantee change, but it makes harmful choices harder to sustain.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: On your money, access, and recognition point, you confuse broad isolation with precise pressure. Decision makers can dodge broad barriers, while workers and families cannot. Targeted measures keep leverage without abandoning everyone else.
